summary: Benidipine is a long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (marketed as Coniel) that blocks L-, T- and N-type calcium channels, used for hypertension, renal parenchymal hypertension and angina pectoris. Despite a short plasma half-life it has a prolonged antihypertensive effect from high affinity for the dihydropyridine binding site, allowing once-daily dosing. It is extensively metabolized by CYP3A4; grapefruit juice and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors raise levels. It is not approved by the US FDA.

moa: Benidipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that inhibits transmembrane calcium influx through L-, T- and N-type voltage-gated calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle and myocardium. This produces arterial vasodilation, reduced peripheral vascular resistance and lower blood pressure, plus coronary vasodilation that relieves angina. Its high affinity for the dihydropyridine binding site on cell membranes confers a long duration of action despite a short plasma half-life.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to benidipine or other dihydropyridines
Severe aortic stenosis (relative to product labeling)
monitor: Symptoms of excessive hypotension (dizziness, flushing, headache)

preg: Benidipine is contraindicated/avoided in pregnancy. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers have shown reproductive toxicity in animals and human safety data are limited. Use only if no safer alternative exists and the potential benefit clearly outweighs the risk; consult an obstetric specialist.
lact: Use during breastfeeding is not recommended; excretion into human milk has not been adequately characterized and dihydropyridines may distribute into milk. Avoid or discontinue nursing during therapy.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment; consider a lower starting dose and gradual titration. Benidipine is primarily cleared by hepatic metabolism with only a small renal contribution, but renal-impaired and renal-parenchymal-hypertension patients should be monitored closely for blood-pressure response and edema.
hepatic: Benidipine is extensively metabolized by hepatic CYP3A4/CYP3A5, so impaired hepatic function may increase exposure. Use with caution, start low and titrate slowly; avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

major: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir) - increased benidipine levels and hypotension
Other antihypertensives and nitrates - additive hypotension
CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine) - reduced efficacy
moderate: Digoxin - calcium channel blockers may raise digoxin levels; monitor
Beta-blockers - additive negative effects on conduction/contractility
Cimetidine - may increase calcium channel blocker exposure
interactions.food: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice (inhibits CYP3A4 and can markedly raise levels). Take the daily dose after breakfast.

serious: Worsening of angina (rare, especially after abrupt withdrawal)

monitoring: Blood pressure and heart rate at baseline and during titration
Liver function in patients with hepatic risk factors
Angina symptom control in patients treated for angina

pk: Gradual; blood-pressure lowering over hours with sustained daily effect
Plasma Tmax approximately 1 to 2 hours after oral dosing
Short plasma half-life (~1 hour); prolonged pharmacologic effect from membrane binding
Long-acting - supports once-daily dosing (twice daily for angina)

pearls: Triple L-/T-/N-type calcium channel blockade may add reno- and cardioprotective effects beyond classic L-type DHPs
Short plasma half-life but long-lasting action due to high affinity for the dihydropyridine membrane binding site - allows once-daily dosing
Extensively metabolized by CYP3A4/3A5 - avoid grapefruit and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
Marketed as Coniel (Kyowa Hakko Kogyo) in Japan and parts of Asia; commonly available as 2 mg, 4 mg and 8 mg tablets
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered on the same day. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the usual schedule - do not double up. For the once-daily regimen, take the next dose after breakfast as usual.
overdose: Overdose may cause marked and prolonged hypotension, reflex tachycardia, flushing, dizziness and, in severe cases, bradycardia or conduction disturbance. Management is supportive: place supine with leg elevation, give intravenous fluids, monitor cardiac rhythm and blood pressure; intravenous calcium, vasopressors and, if needed, atropine may be used for refractory hypotension or bradycardia. Contact a poison control center.
